title: The Deep End
primary_metric: supervised swim-hours accessible to the facility's actual user base (children, seniors, mobility-limited swimmers) per square foot of pool footprint

options.A: The Deep-End Design — a single 8-foot diving well read off a digital depth gauge in whole feet, with dedicated swim-team practice time
options.B: The Zero-Entry Ramp Design — a gradually sloped entry read in tenths of a foot, open to every supervised swimmer at every scheduled hour

sources.claim: ADA accessible-entry requirements for public pools: pools over 300 linear feet of pool wall need at least two accessible means of entry (at least one a sloped entry or lift); smaller pools need only one

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Carla Whitfield, director of the city's only public pool
topic_gap_closed: readmodel/standards_spine.json's last two n==0 skills in Number Sense -- number-sense-depth and number-sense-digit -- both true zero-coverage, elementary-level vocabulary terms. This case exists specifically to close those two gaps.

deliverables.text: A depth-reading table for the Deep-End Design, recording the digital gauge's three posted readings from Appendix A exactly as the gauge displays them (whole feet only), with the pool's maximum depth clearly labeled.

A depth-and-digit table for the Zero-Entry Ramp Design, recording all five posted ramp markers from Appendix B to the nearest tenth of a foot, and for each one, naming the digit in the tenths place and stating what that digit means in real-world terms.

A supervised swim-hours-per-square-foot comparison table for both designs, using the weekly accessible hours and footprint figures in Appendix C, with a one-paragraph recommendation stating which design delivers more supervised swim-hours to the facility's actual user base for the amount of pool footprint it uses.

balance.argument_a: The Deep-End Design uses 23% less pool footprint (2,700 sq ft vs. 3,500 sq ft) to build, permit, and maintain, and it is the only design that gives the city's competitive swim team a dedicated, exclusive practice window (18 hours/week) -- a real, organized constituency with nowhere else in the city to train. Even though its general-access rate per square foot (45 hrs / 2,700 sq ft = 0.01667 hrs/sq ft) trails the ramp design, its absolute weekly footprint and construction cost are both smaller, which matters directly to a council balancing a fixed rebuild budget.
balance.argument_b: The Zero-Entry Ramp Design delivers every one of its 63 weekly scheduled hours to the general supervised user base, with no exclusive-use block carved out, producing a per-square-foot rate of 63 hrs / 3,500 sq ft = 0.018 hrs/sq ft -- a real, computed advantage over the Deep-End Design's 0.01667 hrs/sq ft, even though the ramp's larger footprint costs more to build. It also goes beyond the legal minimum accessible-entry requirement (a portable lift could satisfy that alone) to make every scheduled hour usable by children, seniors, and mobility-limited swimmers without waiting for a lift or a reserved slot.
balance.margin_basis: Rate_A = weekly accessible hours / footprint = (63 - 18) / 2,700 = 45 / 2,700 = 0.016667 hours per square foot. Rate_B = 63 / 3,500 = 0.018 hours per square foot. margin_pct = 100 * (Rate_B - Rate_A) / Rate_A = 100 * (0.018 - 0.016667) / 0.016667 = 8.0%, in the Zero-Entry Ramp Design's favor -- well inside the SPEC §2 20% cap.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Facility's total weekly scheduled supervised-swim hours, and the Deep-End Design's exclusive team-practice block
modeling_assumptions.value_used: 63 hours/week total; 18 hours/week reserved under the Deep-End Design
modeling_assumptions.basis: No engineering or staffing plan exists yet for either design, since the rebuild has not broken ground. 63 hours/week (9 hours/day, 7 days/week) is a common scheduled-hours baseline for a mid-size municipal pool. The 18-hour reserved block reflects a real, common municipal-pool safety practice -- closing general supervised swimming while a diving well is in organized team use, because one lifeguard staff cannot safely cover both a deep diving well and the rest of the pool at the same time -- applied here as a chosen scenario value for this specific facility.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This case's outcome is sensitive to both figures. Changing the reserved-hours block changes only the Deep-End Design's accessible hours; changing the total weekly schedule changes both designs' accessible hours, though not by the same amount, since the reserved block is subtracted from only one of them.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Pool basin footprint for each design, at the shared 30-ft basin width
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Deep-End: 2,700 sq ft; Zero-Entry Ramp: 3,500 sq ft
modeling_assumptions.basis: Zero-entry ramp designs need meaningfully more footprint than a stepped or fixed-depth entry to reach the same swimming depth, because the slope has to descend gradually rather than dropping straight down -- real pool-design guidance describes a typical slope needing roughly 20-25 feet of horizontal entry-zone length to reach standard swimming depth [S3]. This case applies that real design constraint, scaled against the shared 30-ft basin width, to produce the two footprint figures above; the exact figures are this case's own scenario choice, since no site-specific engineering drawing exists yet.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This case's outcome is sensitive to this figure, especially the ramp design's footprint -- it is the single most defensible number in the case for a Hero to challenge, since it depends on a slope requirement this case did not have final engineering drawings to confirm.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: No staffing or operating-hours plan exists yet for the rebuilt facility, since it has not broken ground. 63 hrs/week is a documented good-faith estimate from a common mid-size-municipal-pool scheduling pattern (9 hrs/day, 7 days/week), not a figure this specific facility has published, because it does not exist yet.

No safety/staffing plan has been finalized for the Deep-End Design. 18 hrs/week is a documented good-faith estimate drawn from the common municipal-pool practice of closing general swimming during organized diving-well team use, applied as a scenario value since this exact facility's policy has not been written yet.

No engineering drawing exists yet for the Deep-End Design. 2,700 sq ft is a documented good-faith estimate at the shared 30-ft basin width, since final architectural plans have not been produced for either finalist design.

No engineering drawing exists yet for the Zero-Entry Ramp Design. 3,500 sq ft is a documented good-faith estimate applying real published slope-length guidance [S3] to the shared 30-ft basin width, since final architectural plans have not been produced for either finalist design.

sensitivity_note: This case's 8.0% base margin is genuinely thin: a Tier 2 Probe 5 sweep found the verdict flips (or the margin exceeds the SPEC §2 20% cap) under a +/-50% swing on EACH of the four stated Modeling-Assumption dials (total_weekly_hours, reserved_hours_a, footprint_a, footprint_b -- see sensitivity_disclosure[], all disclosed under Category X: no engineering/staffing plan exists yet for either design, since the rebuild has not broken ground, so each figure is a documented good-faith scenario estimate rather than a number this specific facility has published). This is disclosed, not eliminated, per the disclosure-aware Tier 2 pass state -- the Guide Notes must say the verdict is genuinely fragile, not defend the 8.0% margin as a stable fact. This case also touches disability access and childhood-safety themes -- a one-line facilitator flag per SPEC §6 for the discussion lead, though the stakes here are comparatively low (a civic facility-design decision, not illness or hardship).
